title: Ask what would help a little
description: In a stressful moment, the question “what would fix everything?” paralyses; “what would help a little?” almost always has an answer.

body.heading: Big questions freeze, small questions move
paragraphs: Stress narrows thinking. Faced with a hard situation, the mind demands a complete solution and, finding none available, concludes that nothing can be done. That conclusion feels true and is almost never accurate.

Shrink the question. Not “how do I fix this?” but “what would help a little, in the next hour?” Little is a reachable standard, and reachable standards get answered: a glass of water, a ten-minute walk, sending the email that asks for more time, telling one person the truth about how things are.

body.heading: Help comes in more kinds than solutions
paragraphs: Notice that help is not always action. Sometimes what would help a little is rest. Sometimes it is company, or its opposite. Sometimes it is information, sometimes permission to stop for today, sometimes the dignity of a good cry and a washed face.

Let the answer be honest rather than impressive. On genuinely hard days, “a little help” might be as plain as eating something warm and going to bed early — and that is not a failure of ambition. That is triage, and triage is what sensible people do in real emergencies.

body.heading: Ask it for other people, too
paragraphs: The same question is a gift when someone you care about is struggling. “What would help a little?” respects their knowledge of their own life and asks for something small enough to actually give. It is far easier to answer than “how can I help?” and far more useful than “let me know if you need anything.”

Keep the question in your pocket. It works on deadlines, griefs, messes and Mondays alike — anywhere the gap between the problem and your resources feels too wide for a leap, but just right for a step.

takeaway: When the whole problem is too big, ask the smaller question: what would help a little, now?
